utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning and good day to everyone. Madam Registrar if you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All the accused are here. Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic. Prosecution I see Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. So Ms. Nikolic, can you report progress on the Rule 68 motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The material we expected yesterday has not arrived yet. I've just talked to Mr. Nicholls, and he told me that the disclosure of these documents could be expected by the end of the day today. I hope that will happen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It will be before that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Because we had that statement yesterday. We had that statement the day before. Let's close, let's finish this symphony, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's done, Your Honours. There are four documents similar to the ones that have been disclosed before. I'm told the labels are being put on the CDs right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And my understanding, if I understood you well, yesterday is that if this is done to your satisfaction then you withdraw the motion, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In that case we will withdraw our motion and continue to do the investigation. We also detected some problems with translation yesterday, but I hope they will be resolved too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Later on we will let you know our decision in relation to the same witness, PW-108, but you will get the decision today communicated to you. So yesterday we just started debating the second point that we communicated to you in relation to the admissibility issues on the Borovcanin interview, and the second point is the following, I will repeat it: If the Trial Chamber were to determine that the evidence should have probative value with respect to the other accused, what would be the permissible scope of the submissions on and cross-examination of Witness number 3 - that's Alistair Graham - by the other accused at the stage of the proceedings where admissibility is to be determined. If I remember well, you had very succinctly dealt with this and I think it was determined -- do you wish to say anything? I think Mr. McCloskey had stated something and very briefly, and I'm not quite sure whether he had finished or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I had pretty much finished, but of course giving someone time to think over it over the evening is always dangerous, but I don't really have much else to say, though I do -- I would request that the-- the Trial Chamber have the opportunity to hear the -- the interview before making the decision about whether or not it would be admissible against the other accused. I think that's what you had in mind, but it's from this question that's a little bit unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Who from amongst the Defence teams would like to address this issue, the second question? Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But I suppose those who are more directly or indirectly exposed to this might have. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the event that we get to that point, then I believe that all accused should have the right to fully examine and -- Mr. Graham and make any submissions they feel appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic or Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We take the same position, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic or Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is very ungrateful to speak because it relates to the rights of the other accused. So I will take no position in this respect. I don't think it would be correct from our point to -- to talk about rights of other accused to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but we haven't read the statement of course, we're not aware of its contents, but I have come across in my career many statements which have their pluses and their minuses, statements which could damage the accused making them to some extent and also help the case in others. So you may have an interest to have it admitted in the one context and have the interest in having it thrown out, and that's a decision, of course, that you will take. So the submissions by others may become relevant to you too. Unless, of course, you are all for having it thrown out, declared inadmissible, in which case the submissions of others might help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do hope that that's the situation with all the Defences here today, all would like this statement to not to be added into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my position is the same as that of my colleague, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I enunciated our position yesterday in this regard, Your Honour. I stand by the submissions I've made. I accept them. What I contended yesterday was taking matters to their logical extreme, but in my submission it really is a black and white situation. If the interview has evidential effect against the co-accused, the co-accused are entitled to challenge it totally and in any proper procedural form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Josse. You have crystallized it probably. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, very little to add. The question you ask is what would be the permissible scope, to this extent I do agree with Mr. McCloskey. The permissible scope of the involvement of the co-accused would be to challenge the admissibility of the interview and nothing more. It would not be a general troll through the evidence of Mr. Graham. The one thing I think is absent from your question is that in my submission the other accused would have the right to call evidence on voir dire if they thought there was any that would be relevant. I suppose somebody might want to call Mr. McCloskey, but there it is. But I think the scope of the involvement of the others does include the calling of evidence as well if relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just on more of a procedural issue. The way I would see this happening is that if -- if the initial issue is one of voluntariness. This is not something that I would plan on providing any information from the interview itself, the content of the interview. It would be left to issues of voluntariness which are pretty simple, pretty straightforward. They don't involve -- it will be probably five minutes of direct, and if it's very legal in nature, and in that particular case that is mostly a situation for Mr. Borovcanin's counsel. And as I said yesterday, I do not object if there are legal issues related to other accused. If they announce what those legal issues are. They are able to cross-examine on those issues. Now, after if it's found to be voluntary, if we've met our burden and the it's played or it's admitted one way or another, then it will clearly be in a situation where we now have this document. It will affect the rights of the others and then cross-examination becomes a much more wide-open issue for Alistair Graham. And so that's how -- I'm going on my old experience, but that's how I think it would be best worked out, because otherwise if -- if the wide-open questioning begins in the early stage you don't really have the transcript or the interview to deal with unless there's something specific to voluntariness in the transcript, which then it's fine. But that's the -- that's what I would suggest as -- as one option on how to do this so that we can get the voluntariness issue, which is very specific, out of the way and then get into the more substantive issues of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does anyone wish to comment on that? All right. I think we can now -- yes, Madam Fauveau. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm completely in agreement that it's a very specific situation. However, according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, for a piece of evidence to be admissible it must have probative value. The probative value does not depend only on the voluntariness of any acts of the suspect at the time when he gave that interview or his will alone. It depends also on many other things such as the credibility of evidence. I can see the reasoning of the Prosecutor, but I don't think it is completely consistent with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this Tribunal. I believe we have -- we ought to have the right to test the credibility of this evidence, of this interview, the veracity of its contents, before it is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment Mr. McCloskey. Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, are you suggesting then that prior to admitting the tape we should listen to the entire contents of the tape as a means of determining its probative value?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I believe that certain questions concerning the veracity of the contents can be determined without listening to the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Should you find that the interview was given freely and voluntary, I have no objection to it merely being marked as an exhibit until it's played and cross-examination is done before you make your decision whether it's admissible into Mr. Borovcanin and that I don't think is any problem. And then as for the issue of whether it's admissible against the other accused, I would hope that everyone would have a chance to brief that more fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yesterday I think we made this clear in the first part of the debate in which we stated that without prejudice to the issue of redactions to be dealt with in due course for the purpose of this stage both tape and the transcript will be marked for identification. So I think we premised that before -- before anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's what I thought, which should mean Ms. Fauveau's argument doesn't -- isn't a problem for her or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which doesn't mean to say - I don't want to mislead anyone - it don't mean to say that we will, as soon as these are tendered and marked for identification, that we will jump into reading them if there is no need for us to read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll tell you what we think, and we are unanimous on that, well nearly, when we come to it, Madam Fauveau. Let's move to the third question. If instead we were to determine that this piece of evidence should have no probative value with reference to the other accused, should passages in the interview itself purporting to contain evidence against the other accused be reacted? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Well, the answer to number 3 is no. And as I have divided the interview into three parts, the background, the facts associated with the crimes and acts or conduct of the accused, I believe your question is mostly directed at acts or conducts of the accused. You wouldn't, I don't feel a need to redact one or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I would stick to that, but you're the one who addressed the Trial Chamber yesterday and referred to three different -- three different issues. So I think what I would suggest is that you submit to the Trial Chamber what you feel you ought to submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this is a complex area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I divided it into three areas, as I think we've discussed briefly, as the three different kinds of hearsay, and as we know in 92 bis and our regular hearsay rules don't have a problem really with the first two kinds of -- of hearsay being admitted against an accused. So it's the third kind, the acts or conducts of the accused that -- that is the most serious issue here, and so I would say of course not. You would of course not want to redact the categories one and two. That would make -- well, that would redact the entire interview and make it useless for -- for any purpose. So I think then we need to look at the acts or conducts of the accused that are mentioned in that. Now, I think for this analysis you need to actually fully read and understand those references, but I don't -- for the purposes of today I don't think you do, but I think for the final analysis you would want to. And the reason I say that is because if you found that they were basically valueless or not admissible against -- against anyone else, then as is the foundation of the question, then the question becomes if you redact them, then they're not part of the record. The problem with that is then they become valueless against the man that said them. And as you will look at them, when a person -- if Borovcanin mentions an accused, for example, mentions seeing an accused in a particular place like Potocari, this is something I want you to know when you consider Mr. Borovcanin's case; that he is there in Potocari with another accused. So it does have probative value against Mr. Borovcanin, and so redacting it would be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, then pausing there. If the statement says, "I saw X in Potocari," what is to be redacted is just X. So the fact that Mr. Borovcanin was in Potocari would not be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But the fact that he was there with -- with X at a crime scene and X is at that crime scene and they're charged as joint criminal enterprises, it's very relevant, something I want this court to know, just as if it was a drug case, I would want you to know that X was seen at -- at the scene of the drug distribution place with Y. That's a huge point. This -- this is no different than any criminal case. It's -- in its foundations, and if we have a crime scene, Potocari, I want you to know who is there and who is recognising each other. As -- there is an issue with a meeting as well, though I'm not sure that's even contested by the person it affects, but I think you would need to know that Mr. Borovcanin is at a meeting with another accused, a meeting where issues were discussed, and it may be a hotly contested area. And these things are redacted for juries, Your Honours. This is a jury issue because the law feels that juries cannot separate their emotions from certain facts, and I don't think that's -- that's not a problem this Tribunal has. I don't think there is a lot of lurking jury evidence out there that the Judges are being emotionally swayed by. I don't think that's a problem you will have. And I don't think you want to have these little time bombs in the case, areas that you can't see or can't refer to in your judgement. That's going to make reviewing this case very difficult. And frankly I don't see anything, I don't think you'll see anything in this evidence that is so potentially prejudicial that it's something that you would have a hard time getting out of your mind. It's really -- as I said, Mr. Borovcanin is not blaming anyone, and it's -- but there are references to people that I know you will give it the weight or no weight, if that's what you feel, and I don't -- I don't think that will be a problem. Redacting doesn't really solve any problem. In fact, it would reduce the days against Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Who wishes to -- I'm sorry, Judge Kwon, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is a practice in the Tribunal, including this Chamber, isn't there, that when we are admitting the 92 bis statement without cross-examination we redact some parts relating to the acts and conducts of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We just -- we just did that. As a matter of fact, I think the last witness. But that was something that you decided to do prior to the -- prior to the case, and once we brought those witnesses forward it would have been part of the case. And it's hard for me right now to see the similarity between your decision to redact material prior to the case that we would have to deal with and what we're talking about now, because really to redact the material you would have to fully understand what this material was and absorb it; unless you made the decision, which you could, that any reference to any accused should be deleted. And then you wouldn't -- and then we would give you a redacted format, and that wouldn't be something you've considered, but I think -- well, I don't know what you would prefer, but I think normally it would be the Judges that would -- would review this material to see if -- if it needed to be excluded. In common law jurisdictions many cases are tried with Judges alone and even in those jurisdictions the Judge would review the material, and if he felt it was not admissible he would set it aside. But he wouldn't -- I don't think it would be appropriate for you to wholesale redact something because there was a reference to it, though that's perfectly within your discretion, I believe, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can answer this question in relation to the question put by Judge Kwon in your answer. Basically if you are resorting to the Rule 92 bis procedure, wouldn't that be tantamount on your part to renouncing to the parts -- to the evidence that would otherwise emerge from the redacted parts? Especially if there is no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As I think we just did with a witness. You had decided to react a document that had one of the accused's name on it, and we did not object or take that any further, and we in fact did not even put that document before the witness, and so yes we went along with that -- that process, but that was -- that was for the purposes of 92 bis, for -- to get moving on with the case to -- for efficiency. We didn't think the document was that important. This witness -- that witness on that document didn't have much to say about it. There are other witnesses that had more to say about it. So yes, in a 92 bis situation we would do that, though I don't want to go back in time, I'm still slightly confused that you would have redacted something at the 92 bis stage but require someone for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It shouldn't be redacted if the person is going to be here for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what I'm suggesting is the following as a proposition to which I'll ask you to reply: When you resort to Rule 92 bis, you have no guarantee that the Trial Chamber is going to grant cross-examination. In fact that's one provision where the Trial Chamber is free not to decide not for cross-examination if it doesn't feel there is a need for it. And we have on a consensus precisely done that. But Rule 92 bis precludes you from tendering through the 92 bis process acts which go to the -- parts that go to the acts and conduct of -- of the accused as charged in the indictment. So in that case you would be renouncing to the evidence that that testimony or that testimony would otherwise provide you with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We normally did not present evidence for 92 bis that went to the acts or conducts of the accused knowingly. I think that one situation we feel the document really went to acts or conduct, you disagree with us, so you redacted as was your right. That was a rare item. But what is really different in this context and what is the problem with redaction, redacting what a witness has to say doesn't really affect any other -- it doesn't affect the witness because the witness is not on trial. But when you redact something that an accused said which in our view implicates him, then you are take away from the Prosecution's case and actually affect the case. Taking away something an engineering operator may have said about a document, it doesn't affect any particular -- an accused because no accused was saying it, and we're free to bring in that other evidence in other ways if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in essence I take it what you're saying is the distinction between a 92 bis statement and the statement at issue here is that in 92 bis you can redact in its entirety in reference to all the accused, whereas here you have the situation where the evidence remains relevant to one accused and not relevant to the remaining accused. If that's our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's a more succinct way of what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to concede that I have difficulty in understanding the issue until I actually read the transcript, but I think I can understand your concern as to the redaction of a passage which is related to -- to both accused and to the other co-accused, because if a certain passage is turned out to be a passage solely related to the other accused, having nothing to do with Mr. Borovcanin, then you would not oppose in the redaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I agree with you. We could -- I think this discussion of course is much better had with -- with the sentence in front of us, but in proving criminal intent, what is in a person's mind, what comes out of someone's mouth, through their brain, is a crucial piece of evidence for me. So anything that's coming out of Mr. Borovcanin's mind, especially when he mentions another accused, is something that I want you to see because I think it helps you to get into his mind. Now, I don't have any smoking guns in this regard. We're not -- you know, he's -- I don't want to give you the impression that he's saying something that will solve the issues of the case, but when Mr. Borovcanin identifies an accused at a particular place, then we know that he knows he's with that person or at least in the same place, and that has some value. That has some probative value and helps us prove an issue, at least that he knows that he is there. You may decide that it's not evidence that the other person is there because you may very well find that the other person is putting on evidence that he's not there. But at least it's evidence that Mr. Borovcanin knows someone is -- is there. And that is -- that I think will be important for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us leave it there, and I will hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Who wishes to address the Chamber on this question? Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have nothing but to repeat my position from yesterday, because our position is that no -- no parts of interview could be introduced and are admissible if co-accused has no opportunity to cross-examine the witness. It is our position, and if Mr. Borovcanin decides not to testify in this trial, this part of transcripts -- of his interviews should be redacted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Of course my position is obviously should the Trial Chamber take the position that there is no probative value to any other accused, of course it should be redacted. Mr. McCloskey, in stating that well, no it shouldn't be, is just trying to boot-strap that in or bring it in the back door. I think it -- I find it very interesting that Mr. McCloskey states on at page 5, line 23, that if this tape is played or transcript is admitted, it will affect the rights of the others. He goes on at page 10 to state that -- in answer to a question by Judge Kwon, I believe, that "frankly I don't think you'll see anything in this evidence that is so potentially prejudicial that it's that you will have a hard time putting out of your mind." Well, first he says it will affect the rights of the accused, and then he says, if it comes in, it's really not prejudicial. Well, Frankly if it's really not prejudicial in his mind, why would he object to the redactions? And I think it's especially in this case concerning the Srebrenica tape, which also may be in issue but it's been played and played and played in this courtroom, if Mr. McCloskey says, well, in answer to Judge Kwon's question again, if Mr. Borovcanin hypothetically said that "I saw X at Potocari." Well, then Mr. McCloskey wants you all to believe that this has some probative value to show that Mr. Borovcanin was in Potocari. Well, I think we've seen a tape, have we not, of Mr. Borovcanin in Potocari. It should be redacted, otherwise it's an exercise in futility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I have a question to you. If we are redacting some parts at all then who should decide to redact and how? If there's a disagreement among the parties, they should have a look at the transcript and look. What would you say to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's a very good question, Your Honour. I believe, should you make that decision, I believe that it would be a very simple proposition and exercise for Mr. McCloskey and the Defence counsel for the other accused to be able to agree on the redactions. And just to give you an idea: If you all rule correctly and you find that there is no probative value and there should be redactions, and I can even whittle this down further, in this transcript I would be requesting -- and again it can be whittled down quite a bit, a lot, actually, only 48 lines out of approximately 6.300 lines. Now -- and that's lines, Judge Kwon. That's not as you suggested earlier just a name. So if you want to just take a name out, for example, it would be a lot less than that. Now, 43 -- hypothetically 48 lines out of approximately 6.300 will not change the substance of -- otherwise change the substance of what Mr. Borovcanin said if you allow and find that was an admissible voluntary statement and should go into evidence against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You seem to be agreeing now with the part of Mr. McCloskey's statement that you contested a couple of minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Which part would that be, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The second part of his statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the second part of his statement. You -- from page 10, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Oh, from page 10?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You suggested that Mr. McCloskey was sort of contradicting himself, for saying that it would have importance for all the accused, and then you suggested that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, I just pointed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't agree with that at all. I'm pointing that he's on both sides of the fence. First he tells you the one thing, that oh, you know, and he says it's not so prejudicial. Why he would care? That's the Prosecution state of mind. I'm telling you perhaps it might not be prejudicial, but still I have a right and a duty to represent my client and make sure he has a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not being contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Without going into fair trial, et cetera, and no, don't agree with that, and I'm just pointing out that that's what he stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. No one is contesting that this is important for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, can you explain to me why you feel it -- why do you feel it's necessary for those redactions to be made? Is it your position that the Trial Chamber is not able to separate the evidence in terms of its relevance to Mr. Borovcanin and its relevance to the other accused should we rule that it's not of probative value to the other accused? Is it your evidence that we're not able to do that separation process and that's the need for the redactions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My position is if there is no probative value and it's not going to be used towards the other accused, whether you can put it out of your minds or not, why even have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That begs the question that Mr. McCloskey referred to and which you haven't answered; namely, that Mr. McCloskey told you granted for argument's sake that certain excerpts which go to the acts and conducts of the other accused are not to be made use of vis-a-vis the other co-accused. Still in those excerpts, in those parts, there is information or there could be information or facts which are relevant for the person, for the accused, who made that statement. And you haven't actually dealt with that except that you said here, but we're talking of his presence in -- alleged presence in Potocari you have other evidence. But you can't argue the point by means of one isolated example or instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what you need to argue is whether there is any validity or not in the argument or in the submission made by Mr. McCloskey, namely, that granted that those parts will not have any probative value vis-a-vis the other co-accused. Why should I be deprived from making use of what is contained in those parts for my case against the accused who made that statement? All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Your Honour, and I have had a chance to review and read this interview, and in my opinion, in my submission as an officer of the court, anything that I would ask to be redacted should you make a ruling that it's not probative to other accused, I submit, Your Honour, would have no affect on the Prosecution's case against Mr. Borovcanin, period. That's what I'm trying to tell you. I mean, that's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I'm not sure whether you answered to my question in full. As for those 48 lines you referred to, if Mr. McCloskey would not agree with you, then we Judges should read those parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would have to agree with you. If we came to an impasse on certain redactions after a line or a sentence or a word or two words, then, yeah, I believe that would have to go to the Chamber, but that's a bridge I don't think we have to cross at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Judge Kwon is a hundred per cent right. Already there is an impasse. So -- so you need to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My next question is that being the case, Judge -- with Judges having read those passages already, what's the point of redacting that part later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Judge Kwon, in answer to your question, you're absolutely right. You're absolutely right. If that's what's going to happen, then why are here arguing this right now? It's an exercise in futility. And we had another issue with a long document, and it took us some time, but we did get the redactions completed and it got admitted, and it didn't entail having it to bring it to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you're speaking of Eileen Gilleece's statement. I'm not sure we're there yet. We're getting closer and we're doing the process you're describing, but we may be at an impasse on that one as well, but we have entered into this process before. We understand the Court has done similar things. So -- but I think we're definitely at an impasse with this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is -- there is another problem. Mr. Meek is fast on the draw. So let's proceed. Mr. Meek, I don't think you can assume that there will be an agreement in whole or in part about possible redactions. I think you for the time being, in trying to answer the very pertinent questions that were put to you by Judge Kwon, you have to assume exactly the contrary, the opposite, in other words that there will be what you called an impasse, which would be the position you have reached now, already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's where I disagree with you. If you want to take the position and a state of mind that yes there will be an impasse, because Mr. McCloskey says, oh, yes, there will be an impasse, I don't believe that and I'll tell you why. Because Mr. McCloskey has always dealt with us, I believe in an honest fashion and aboveboard. If an order comes from [indiscernible] that there should be redactions, I believe in good faith that he will not take the position and nothing is going to be redacted and we can't agree on this word or those words. That's just what I believe, Judge. So, yes, if you all want to take the position that, yes there will be an impasse, yes we're going to have to look at it anyway, then you can take that position. The glass is either half full or half empty. Well, I believe we can work it out if you make that ruling. If you make the ruling and we can't work it out, then yes someone's going to have to look at it for the Trial Chamber but why presume that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could watch out with your sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's just as easy, Your Honours, to presume that should you issue an order that the Prosecution will act in good fate. And that's my submission. Now, if you want to take the position that - and this is pure speculation that if you make such an order - that they're not going to agree with us on every little thing and it's going to have to come back to you, then I guess you could say, okay forget it. We're just going to look at it, but that's up to you. I believe if you enter and reach that we can -- we can reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Meek. Ms. Nikolic or Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. As you well know it has been since the beginning of trial a sensitive issue as to whether we should allow the Judges to see some material or not to see some material. I believe that in this case we have the two options. Either we proceed with no redactions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. I object to you using -- maybe you didn't use these words intentionally, but the idea whether we should allow the Judges to see. You have -- it has never been and it will never be a question of you -- either of the two sides allowing the Judges to see. That's for us to decide, not for you to allow us to -- to see or not. Okay. Let's make that clear. Any time -- any time we can surprise you and tell you from now on we're going to see all documents, all previous statements of witnesses, all -- everything, and it is within our rights to do that. And it's not within your rights to allow us not to do that. So let's make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my English is not good enough. Maybe I should be speaking French, because when I say should allow, I do not mean in any way, respectfully put, that we are to decide anything in this courtroom, and if I ever referred this way, and if you ever had the impression that referring that we could decide on something, well, then I apologise, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Bourgon. The important thing is -- because this is the second time we have had to draw your attention. This is the second time that we had to draw your attention, when I say yours, it's not necessarily you as Mr. Bourgon, because it has been stated by others as well but it's the second occasion that we've had to make this clear. This is something that we have decided at the beginning of the case to adopt as a practice. It's not a rule that we have imposed upon ourselves with -- without -- without any option to go back on it. So I -- but I do appreciate that it was a -- maybe a slip of the tongue, slip -- language. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Thank you, Mr. President. The issue is twofold, either we proceed with redactions or we proceed without redactions and the ruling of the Trial Chamber I assume would be accompanied by what exactly is meant to be done with the portions that are relevant to both Mr. Borovcanin and some other accused. As a preliminary matter, I must say that this issue does not concern my client and I am speaking simply on the matter of principle. I believe that what is important, Mr. President, is what exactly will accompany the ruling from the Trial Chamber. What position will the Trial Chamber take with respect to an issue or part of the statement of Mr. Borovcanin that also affects another accused? And if that ruling is precise and we know exactly what the Trial Chamber will do, then I guess we can proceed without redactions. However, it is my view that it is much safer to proceed with redactions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon, but why would it be much safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is much safer because in the end when we have a judgement once this case is over and then there is a doubt in the mind of any of the accused representing -- any of the counsel representing any of the accused that what the use that has been made of Mr. Borovcanin's statement is not in accordance with what should have been done, then there's a possibility that this might be a ground of appeal. If we have redactions that were made out of consent between the Prosecution and the Defence, in such a case we know exactly what has been considered and what has not been considered. So it's just a matter of being much safer. But that can be overcome, Mr. President, by clear guidance from the Trial Chamber as what is the use of a statement that affects that effects both Mr. Borovcanin and another accused. And the example that was used, Mr. Borovcanin saw X in Potocari, I think it's a benign example, but it's also a good example. Because if it is left unredacted for the purposes explained by Mr. McCloskey that the Trial Chamber knows that he had this in his mind, that he saw another accused, or if we just redact the name of the accused, then what will be the value of this exact statement for another accused? That's the important part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that can be made clear by the Trial Chamber, and then in this sense we would proceed with no redactions. And again, Mr. President, if I ever gave you the impression --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's important for me, Mr. President, because that's a number of times that I believe that I'm being taken aside, that I'm being pointed out by the Trial Chamber for statements that I make in this Trial Chamber, I respectfully say that it is not my intention, it has never been my intention, and I believe there's only one Bench in this courtroom, and you make all the decisions. That being said, if you think I say something wrong, and if you want to take me out of this courtroom, then do so. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honours, I don't believe that this is something that we shall interfere with because it relates strictly to other Defences and the situation in which other Defences are affected by some parts of Mr. Borovcanin and the admissibility. Whether it should be redacted or not, I leave it to my colleagues. But I may suggest they try to get find an agreement with the Prosecution. Once they see both sides, the Prosecution and the Defences, what is the extent of such proposed redactions maybe the answer to your question will -- will be dealt with without any further comments on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but Mr. Lazarevic, I beg to differ on the first part of your statement. The suggestion that the Prosecution made in the first place was assuming for argument's sake after that the Trial Chamber has decided that the relevant parts involving or relating to other co-accused will not carry any probative value or will not be used vis-a-vis those other co-accused, the Prosecution is telling you, still I don't want them redacted, because in them there is evidence that goes to either the frame of mind of your client or the participation of your client, and reference was made to joint criminal enterprise in particular. So I disagree with you that this is a matter -- redaction is a matter that concerns your colleagues or the respective clients of your colleagues and not your own client. It does concern your client. What the Prosecution is precisely claiming is no redactions, please, because those are important for my case against Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. In this way it is put in another way that maybe I didn't understand properly. I was listening very carefully to what Mr. McCloskey said, and basically from the very beginning it was the only position that we have that not any part of the interview should be entered into. And so now we are we are talking about the separate issue, whether some redactions are needed, but in a situation that the Trial Chamber decides that no part of the interview will have effect toward other clients. So then I'm going back to the first issue. Whatever the Trial Chamber decision is on this it basically affects -- both situation affects Mr. Borovcanin, and if the Trial Chamber decides not to deal with the interview at all, not to admit it into interview [sic], then we will have no such discussion. If the Trial Chamber decides that the redactions are needed then I will -- I will turn back to my -- to the initial proposal that I just said. It should be meted out between these two parties. Of course, whatever Mr. Borovcanin has said in interview regarding some, some incidents, some situation that appeal, I don't want to go into substance of his interview, is of course related to him. But of course in such a situation, being part of -- well, I'm not suggesting that he was part of any joint criminal enterprise, but he's charged as, the Defence of Mr. Borovcanin would only benefit if certain parts of the interview would be redacted. So this is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. The point made by the Prosecution and we understood by everyone is if there is a total redaction of these parts that would be beneficial to all involved accused and co-accused, but the benefit that your client would derive from is -- would be unduly derived. This is basically what has been submitted. So I take it that you are also pretty much in favour of redactions as the previous speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam -- yes, Mr. McCloskey. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'll wait my turn. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's certainly because of my continental law culture that I'm used to professional Judges, and I'm not used to redactions. However, I must admit that in this particular case it don't concern my client because his name doesn't appear in the interview. Otherwise, my position would have been different if my client's name had been mentioned. What I would like to say now is the following: If we listened to what Mr. McCloskey said carefully, I think he has just answered a question put yesterday: Why is this particular hearsay different from other forms of hearsay, because he made a very important distinction between this interview and the statements that were admitted into this process under 92 bis. And as far as redaction are concerned, I would also add -- I'll repeat once again that I certainly don't have any problem having certain parts redacted, but it's true that the Chamber adopted this practice of redaction in statements that were admitted under 92 bis. And I'm also aware of the fact that the Chamber in this case had access to those statements. So I have no solution to this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our submission the answer to the question is no. However, I repeat what's been said by a number of my predecessors; namely, it isn't really a question that affects my client greatly if at all, and therefore it's easy for me to say no. I am aware that others regard the matter with more sensitivity. That's understandable, and I don't want to tread on their toes unduly. However, where I disagree radically with my learned friend Mr. McCloskey is in his categorisation because again in my submission the matter needs to be dealt with logically. And if category 3 is or might be redacted, we submit there is no logical or legal reason why categories 1 and 2 of his definition should also not be redacted. Of course I then recognise that the logical result of that is there will be virtually nothing left of Mr. Borovcanin's interview. However, I do submit that if the Trial Chamber is going to contemplate redacting category 3, then it should also redact categories 1 and 2 which do have some effect against my client, hence the reason Mr. McCloskey has been arguing as strongly as he has that the interview is admissible as against my client and indeed all the other defendants in the dock in this particular case. Your Honour, it's also easy for me to say, but realistically this is a trial being conducted by a Judge alone. You and your colleagues wear two hats. One is of Judges of the fact. The other is the Judges of the law. The fact is on occasions you have to see material which you might then need to put out of your mine. On behalf of General Gvero, we accept and understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Josse. One moment. Have you decide -- have you changed your mind? Don't you want to wait for your turn now, Mr. McCloskey? There's still Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know how I forgot Mr. Haynes. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Flattery. Flattery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to be repetitive, but perhaps I might pick up on a point that Mr. Meek began to make until he realised he was in error, and that is the question of the as-yet unresolved aide-memoire of Eileen Gilleece. It's perhaps worth bearing in mind that in relation to that piece of evidence which is, I suppose, an interview of my client, the Prosecution have already conceded that portions that affect other accused in this trial ought to be redacted, and so I repeat a question which Mr. Josse has already put to Mr. McCloskey, what has changed now? Why is it that what Mr. Pandurevic might have to say about other accused ought to be redacted from the Eileen Gilleece aide-memoire, yet what Mr. Borovcanin has to say about other accused is not to be redacted from the transcript of his interview. I'll repeat another point that's been made, and I hope just to make it more clearly. The question of the redactions of Mr. Borovcanin's interview are a storm in a teacup. I don't want any redactions from his interview, and I don't believe many more than one accused here wants redactions from his interview. Both the Prosecution and the lawyers for that accused know what those passages are. I think they've already been notified. And the suggestion that there might be some impasse reached, although a possibility we have to face is in reality not likely to arise. If it does arise, of course we will have to ask your help. You are the Judges of the law in this case, and you would have to resolve the issue. You're the only place we can come to. But even in the event we have to do that, there should still be redactions. Why? Because the law has to -- I'm sorry, justice has to appear to be done. We know you can put it out of your mind, but the public don't. The accused don't. The accused who might go to separate lawyers and seek an appeal against your verdict don't know that. If you decide that assertions by Mr. Borovcanin about the involvement of other accused are not probative against them. It makes no sense to keep that written record on the record of this trial. For appearance's sake should you redact it. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Now you have your say, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As you are aware, and we of course did involve you and alert you to the Eileen Gilleece situation. That is an ongoing effort of the parties to agree to something, and if we can't agree, we may be in taking the position that we're taking now, that it all comes in. It's -- there's fundamentally different things that are said in that interview and of a much different nature than the things that are said by Mr. Borovcanin and that is something that we were cognisant of, and that's why we're discussing that with the Defence. It was also not a taped interview, as you know. So we'll see how that goes and we'll inform you, of course. I agree with Mr. Josse that you should be reviewing this material before any redactions are made or even suggested. That's crucial on a -- on one very practical level. For example, if Borovcanin said something like someone was at Potocari, and you told us without looking at that to delete who he mentioned, and if another lawyer got up and said, "That doesn't affect my client," then you would be left one of -- which accused may it have mentioned, and that could be a problem to the accused that was not mentioned in Potocari. So you're getting in this -- and I know you're not going to do guessing games, but the evidence that is mentioned that goes to the acts or conduct of the accused is largely corroborated by other evidence and will not, by accident, if you review it, suggest somebody else was at Potocari that we don't have evidence that it was. So it's really important if you review this material. If you decide you need to redact it that's within your discretion obviously, but I don't think there's anything in there that requires the public not to see it or in fact I think it may be the reverse. I think the public should see as much as they can in this trial. And the idea that -- I take it Mr. Josse was developing the common law adversarial system and finding a technical way of throwing out the entire interview, which I obviously object to strongly, but I can put on my adversarial hat and say that we're at a point in this trial where they have waived their right to even make this argument because that's an argument you make at joinder, because if at joinder the statement gets thrown out, then I withdraw joinder and I try Mr. Borovcanin by himself. But once a case is joined without anyone challenging that statement, I have the, in the adversarial system, the right to stand on that and they have waived their right. Now, I am not bringing up the adversarial system which we know is based on trial by combat in all its intricacies to try to exclude this statement or try to include it at this point, I'm not making that argument, I don't think those arguments should be made and they are not arguments appropriate at this level. But in any event, enough said. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the fact -- a practical difficulty I anticipate if we are not to redact any part related to the other accused is that we have to divide our deliberation or way of thinking with respect to accused. If we are to delete, we are to disregard that part of evidence in relation to all the accused, that's easy. I think we can do that. But although we are professional Judges, but as a human being how can you disregard those parts which is we are going to use in relation to one accused in relation to other accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- I understand that issue, and that's partly why we're in discussions with Mr. Haynes on the interview of Eileen Gilleece, because that is going to be a tricky business in that particular interview, but I'll go back to a phrase from our adversarial law that I was reminded in listening to Mr. Meek and I think it will bring fond memories of him, it probably gets mentioned in every trial I've ever been in, and that is we're offering evidence not for the truth of the matter asserted, but to the state of the mind of the declarant. And this is an instruction that gets given to juries every day and Judges ask them to do it. It can be difficult, because I think it's something that you -- that you can do if you need to. I don't think because of the structure of this system and the admissibility of hearsay that you need to at all. I think it should all go to weight. And so you can give it any consideration you want, and you can decide to give it none if you want and then -- as a Judge I would find it simpler in the end to look at it that way, because then when your judgement's being reviewed no one is going to be able to say, ah they've redacted that, but look in their judgement it appears as if they've considered it, which will be a classic way of challenging any judgement. So, yes, it's a difficult job and I'm happy that -- that it's your job and not mine, but I don't -- I think it's eminently doable in this context and again it's just so important why you need to see this and so we can discuss the various sentences because, I think when we get to that, I think you'll find it a much easier job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My final question -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On this point Mr. Meek if you have anything to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes I have one thing to say and I certainly have heard that quite often where I practice, but Mr. McCloskey can't sit here and tell you that if in this interview hypothetically Mr. Borovcanin said, "I was at location X and I saw Joe Blow," that that had anything whatsoever to do with Mr. Borovcanin's state of mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll ask later if any. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In relation to Your Honour Judge Kwon's question, of course there is one huge advantage in trial by Judge from an accused's point of view; namely, at the end of the trial the accused will get reasons as to why he or she has been found guilty or not guilty and that will be dealt with count by count, particular by particular. And that is in my view a huge advantage over a jury trial where all the accused knows, particularly if he's been found guilty, is that he has been found guilty and the jury is aren't giving any reasons for being found guilty. However, that is caveat to that in relation to what my learned friend, Mr. McCloskey, has just said. Namely, it's all very well to say, well, you the professional Judges can sort it out later, so long as at the end of the case the accused are told in terms evidence by evidence, exhibit by exhibit, what weight you have given to each of those exhibits. Well, that of course in this case, like really any case in this Tribunal, would be a mammoth task, a mammoth task because each case has so many exhibits and so many pieces of evidence in it. That for you in the course of a judgement break down what weight you've given to each particular evidence and in particular what weight you've applied it to each of the seven accused is a huge task as I've already said, and if you think and I say this with the greatest of respect, that is a manageable task then what Mr. McCloskey says is fair and fine, but if not, it does have practical implications and it goes back to the issue of the admissibility of this particular interview as against the seven other accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse, but my concern was that whether any part of the evidence which was used against certain accused can have any bearing upon whether -- whether or not to believe other exhibits to be used against the other accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, there is no question, I submit, that you are trying seven men, and in effect there are seven cases here that have been joined for the sake of convenience, and it is by no reasons inconceivable, certainly in the common law system, even with a jury this happens always time, that you may conclude there are certain pieces of evidence which only goes as against one accused, and in the end it is possible that there isn't a coherent jigsaw so far as the seven accused are concerned, because ultimately all you need to say is whether you're satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that a given accused is guilty on a given count. If you are not satisfied, then of course the verdict is not guilty. The point I'm trying to make is is that there may not be a coherent picture in relation to all seven accused. Now, whilst that's a difficult concept, it's a perfectly logical one, and in particular, it's one the accused are not prejudiced by because you are going to have to give reasons. I hope that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm still musing, but can I ask a final question to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You answered to my previous question that if we are to redact some part of the -- Mr. Borovcanin's statement, then we will lose that part which is also related to Mr. Borovcanin. Can we not view that kind of result as a consequence of joinder? By joining the accused you are to lose some part of the evidence inevitably. What do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with you absolutely, and while I won't get into the -- counsel's invitation on Mr. Jokic, that one of the reasons we took the position we took in Mr. Jokic was for that -- that concern. But that in the adversarial system is a decision that's decided at the joinder motion stage, and so the Prosecution has the opportunity to evaluate whether he wants to go forward alone or he wants to go forward with a redacted version. Since it was not challenged at the -- as far as I recall, at that stage under an adversarial system, they would be prevented from bringing it up. I think when we go over these statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. You say it was decided in the joinder motion stage? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One reason not to grant to anyone that objected to joinder should have said, "We object to joinder because Mr. Borovcanin's statement will be -- will come into evidence, and it will affect my client and negatively." That is a ground for severance or lack of joinder in an adversarial system, because the jury -- many times you don't want to give the jury an instruction ignore what he said against him. The problem you pointed out. That's a ground for joinder. And if you don't bring it up at joiner, the Prosecution doesn't have -- if it's not brought up at joinder it's waived to be brought up later on. Now, that's a technical adversarial system which I'm not trying to bring upon us. I'm very willing to argue this now. But that's what I was referring to. But again, once we get to these phrases, and I don't have them all in my head, some of them may not really affect Mr. Borovcanin, though most of them do because he said them, but others might. And I do agree with Mr. Meek, if you do give us an order, we'll of course be able to work these things out as we have for 10 months now. I think -- we may not, but I think we will be able to, but I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see if I am understood you well. Judge Kwon's question was very simply put as follows: Can we not view that kind -- or that as a kind of result as a consequence of the joinder? By joining the accused, you are to lose some part of the evidence inevitably. So your answer to that is no, Judge Kwon, it's exactly the opposite. Once the matter was not raised the during the joinder stage, as far as you are concerned, it's a matter that assumes a legal existence because according to you the Defence teams, the accused, cannot raise it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's -- that's correct. I think Judge Kwon is correct that it would be an issue at the joinder stage that I would have to live with, like you suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- but -- but the nature of an adversarial system means that I should not have to live with it after the joinder is made. Standing here now whether I want to throw the adversarial system at you in that particular context; frankly my answer is I don't. So I'm not suggesting that that has been waived and that can't be discussed right now. I'd rather -- I think we can discuss it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I wanted to --.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think if you take that into account overall that it wasn't brought up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to see clear into that. Madam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My point is on -- I'm waiting for my -- my point was that the -- the other way around on your part would be also possible. By joining you may have consequences of not using part of the accused's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, and I could -- at the time that that was discussed, I could have constructed the statement around any legal problems to make joinder possible, especially when there's not 50 other courtrooms that I could try him in and 200 other Judges. And we could have constructed it around that had that been the case but since it wasn't brought up, there was no reason to do any construction. Also, you'll see the statements. I'm not sure there's a whole lot of reasons to do any construction anyway but, yes that -- that would have been a function of joinder, but it should have been decided at the time of joinder. I don't have any problem with it now, and I hope it's not a burden I have now as part of this debate, but I'm willing to take it if it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Madam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I find the arguments of the Prosecutor rather interesting concerning joinder, because it's in fact the Prosecutor who asked for joinder. We the Defence of General Miletic were opposed. We appealed against the decision on joinder, and one of the grounds of our appeal was in fact that the leading of evidence against co-accused could be prejudicial to General Miletic. This argument did not concern in particular the interview of Mr. Borovcanin because I don't think we were even aware of its existence at the time, and we were certainly not away, because even today it's not on the 65 ter list, but we were in any case not aware that it was ever going to be admitted into evidence. What I'm trying to say is that in a joint trial the accused should have all the rights, would have the right to be tried the same way as if he were being tried separately. If General Miletic were being tried separately, it is certain that the Borovcanin interview would never enter into evidence in his trial, as it shouldn't now. And in any case, contrary to what the Prosecutor says, in keeping with Article -- Rule 82, something can be excluded. An instruction by the Court can be made at any time during the trial if the rights of the accused are thereby jeopardised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much Madam Fauveau and also -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly to clear the record. I'm sure she was aware of the statement. And it is -- contrary to what she has said, that interview does affect her client, and it will be argued that it affects her client, and it will also to some but a lesser degree affect General Gvero, to a lesser degree, but just so you know that. Again we're arguing in a vacuum because we don't have it, but -- and I don't want to argue that now, but it's the third time she's said that, so I had to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think it's the time to close the -- bring the sit to go an end. I wish to thank you all for your contribution on -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can I have 30 seconds [realtime transcript read in error "minutes"] to make a point on PW-108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will be very brief. I agreed with the Defence request and did not object to their request for more time because they told me in good faith they needed more time to investigate. And the reason I agreed really one other than just to cooperate was because it's very important that the witness not have to come here once and then go home and then come back again. And they assured me that they thought they would be asking for more time if he did come. So I just wanted to say that I don't object to more time, but what I hope Your Honours don't decide to do, and I would strongly urge you not to do is to bring him in just for direct examination or just for a portion of cross and then return, I think. Because of the security concerns we strongly suggest that this witness come here on one occasion only. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for the record of page 41, line 5, Mr. Nicholls didn't ask for 30 minutes, 30 seconds. Okay. I wish to thank you all for your contributions to the debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25-minute break now, and after which we'll come back to you on PW-108, because we still are undecided what to do, and we need to reach consensus on that. That's number one. And the second thing, we will give you a directive -- direction as to what's going to happen on Tuesday when Mr. Alistair Graham comes over. In other words, whether in addition to Mr. Borovcanin, as lawyers, whether the -- other counsel, other counsel would be -- would have the opportunity to cross-examine the witness on admissibility issues as well. So that the reason being that you need to be prepared for this before he actually comes to give testimony, give evidence. So 25 minutes from now we'll come back on these two issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to clarify something in the transcript. On page 40, line 14, when I said Article 82, I said that a joinder case could be separated, and in the transcript it says something can be exploded [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other thing I wanted to point out is that I never said that the interview had no influence or I impact on my client. I said his name wasn't mentioned in the interview, and as a result redaction doesn't concern him; but I didn't refer to the interview itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if people had noticed the existence of that word in the transcript we probably would not be sitting now. So let me come first to the -- what would have been the next witness, PW-108. As you may have guessed before, we were a little bit hesitant on this. However, we do understand your concerns, Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Bourgon, and also your concern, Mr. Nicholls, that you wouldn't like to have this person's testimony in -- in bits and pieces or with hiccups or with interruptions, so ultimately we have come to the decision that we will cooperate with you. So for the time being we will be postponing the testimony as per your request, Ms. Nikolic. Next item that we are going to deal with is what I anticipated before -- immediately before the break, and that's giving you a directive, a direction as to what's going to happen when Mr. Alistair Graham shows up on Tuesday. As regards examination and cross-examination. It had been the Trial Chamber's original intention to decide the issue of Borovcanin's statement if admitted with reference to the other accused prior to the testimony of Alistair Graham next -- which is due next week. However, given the extent of the submissions and the witness schedule problems, that will not be feasible. As stated yesterday, however, there will be a two-stage process in relation to the Borovcanin statement with the first stage relating solely to admissibility. As a result, I'm afraid that on this occasion the Prosecution, taking prompt from Mr. Josse's expression, which I had used before, too, on another occasion, the Prosecution will neither have the cake nor be able to eat it. As we have decided to reserve our decision on the use of the statement against the co-accused, we are going to allow all Defence counsel to cross-examine and make submissions on the admissibility of the interview. However, there are some caveats. First, the Borovcanin Defence team will necessarily and obviously be the first to proceed with cross-examination and then they will be followed by other Defence teams in the order that you may wish to choose amongst you, amongst yourselves. As usual, however, no repetition will be allowed in terms of questioning or submissions, and even more importantly, the questioning should at this stage be restricted to the issue of admissibility of the statement. This, as indicated yesterday, will be the case for both the Prosecution and the Defence. Finally on the broader issue of the use of the statement, if any of the parties wish to supplement the extensive submissions made yesterday, that is in -- in other words, on whether relevant parts could be made use of vis-a-vis co-accused. So if you wish to supplement the extensive submissions yesterday or provide any additional case authorities, then we are giving you the opportunity to do this provided it's filed by close of business on Friday the 20th of July. And that disposes of the matter for the time being. Of course it's only the first part or the first chapter that we have written, and we'll take it up from there in due course. Now, do you wish to raise anything else before we adjourn? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't anticipate playing any parts of the tape regarding admissibility on direct examination. Perhaps on redirect if -- if it is brought up on cross. Should we be prepared after the voluntariness/admissibility issue is decided to -- to play the rest of the tape, or is that something you don't want to hear, or where do we go from there? And I -- I have had requests from the press that they would like to hear the material, too, because they want to know what's being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't do things here because others request them. Let me confer with my colleagues, please, on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't know if you've ever been a Boy Scout, Mr. McCloskey, but if you haven't, we suggest that you become one, and a good one at that. So our answer to that is be prepared. We don't know what will be the position during or at the end of Mr. Graham's testimony. We may or we may not require. So be prepared for either of the two eventualities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I -- I will be. I can recite the Scout oath, but I think that's about it. Can I ask you one more -- one more question? The -- as, I you know you've been listening to me far too much, probably, but I have been suggesting that the issue for Alistair Graham's testimony at first is an issue of the legal issue of voluntariness, and now you have -- have ruled that the issue will be admissibility. Now, admissibility, as we know from the intercepts, can be much broader than voluntariness. It can go to the reliability, credibility of Alistair Graham, I guess, of questions he asked, and because normally a voluntariness voir dire is very short and is pretty much limited to very certain specific issues that go to voluntariness, but if my understanding that this is -- goes to admissibility, a much broader topic, then they're able to cross-examine on an a much broader topic than -- than voluntariness. The -- our intention for what we did on -- in our direct examination may -- may change. So in fact if it's a full frontal, full attack on reliability, credibility as we've seen your decisions relating to the intercepts, it may make, well, more sense from the Prosecution's perspective for you to see this product before the attack. If it's a full attack, you had should see the product before the attack, and -- but if it's a limited voluntariness issue, you see, you see the person in charge of voluntariness, the investigator, and he's challenged by everyone. So if it's a full attack on the whole process, on the whole interview, the best way to do that would be to see the whole interview and then attack the whole interview. What I was suggesting was the voluntariness issue first. If the voluntary hurdle is met, then the document -- it should be admissible against Borovcanin and it should be accepted into court against him, and then the issue of acceptance against others could be argued. And if overall credibility of the overall document -- or interview was going to be challenged, then we'd play the tape at the point and then all the cross-examinations occur. But I don't think it's fair to have a challenge to this entire product without you seeing the product first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse and Mr. Lazarevic. I think I'll give the floor to Mr. Lazarevic first. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe it has to do with it. What we suggest, after I heard what Mr. McCloskey said is that he's trying to put these interviews through the back door in this way. The way we understand it, if Mr. McCloskey intends to play the tape before a decision of this Trial Chamber is issued about the admissibility of the interviews, that would cause serious prejudice against not just Mr. Borovcanin but against -- but towards all the other of the accused. So it is our position - I apologise - that first a decision about the admissibility of the interviews should be decided by this Trial Chamber, and I have to say at this moment if the Trial Chamber decides that these interviews should be added into evidence, we will ask for certification against such an appeal. I believe Your Honour had already anticipated this I believe a day or two ago when we had similar discussion. You told us that whatever the decision on admissibility would be, either the Prosecution or the Defence would appeal against it. So I'm strongly objecting of playing tapes before the question of admissibility is decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make this different practical observation, Your Honour, in relation to Mr. McCloskey's plea as to whether he needs to be prepared.
